Ok so, a quick ELI5: why was southern Michigan hit so much harder by the decline of manufacturing than the rest of the rust belt?

I remembered this being posted on deddit a while ago. I can't vouch for the accuracy of it, but you may find it useful/interesting:

It would be hard to explain without writing a whole book but i'll try to keep it short. Detroit's decline can be chalked up to a perfect storm of racism, suburbanization, and economic decline. Detroit in its prime had 1.8 million people and was the 4th richest city in the country with the highest per capita income. If the American dream was to have a car, a family, and a house with a white picket fence then in Detroit you had all that plus a boat and a place out in the country side. In those times the US was in a golden age of manufacturing and Detroit was at its very center. During WW2 the government refitted our factories and Detroit claimed the title of "The Arsenal of Democracy" (along with absurd amounts of cash from the gov). After the war many Americans returned home and in 1944 the GI bill was passed that gave benefits such as low interest mortgages for homes and businesses as well as paid collage tuition. From this point on, everything went down hill.

Black Americans who left the south, fleeing from jim crow came to northern cities in search of low education jobs in manufacturing, however white families were non to pleased. racial tensions soared and even full riots broke out. It wasn't uncommon for half the street to put up a for sale sign if just one black family moved down the block. Many politicians built their careers around that fear and would continue to do so all the way up until the mid 90's (google L. Brooks Patterson for an example if you feel so inclined). This has created a DEEP divide between the city and the suburbs that has made regional growth damn near impossible (though things have gotten significantly better in the last few years but i'll get to that later). I think its worth noting that, Oddly enough, racial tension has been limited to a white/black issue. Detroit had a reputation of accepting eastern Europeans since the 1880's, we have also had a large Arab community that dates back to the 20's (fun fact; Ford preferred Muslim workers because of their sobriety).

By the 50's Detroit and most Midwest cities had reached their climax and it was at this point that Detroit's massive personal wealth and automotive nature became a curse. In 1956 the Eisenhower administration passed the Federal Highway Act that gouged Detroit and destroyed many neighborhoods, most of which were "coincidentally" black neighborhoods. GM's streetcar scandal came to fruition and effectively dismantled most of America's mass transit to sell more cars. What happens when you have lots for cheap land, lots of money, and only cars to get around? You get massive suburbanization. White families fled across 8 Mile (the boarder of Detroit) and flooded into near by villages that were now connected via highways. The loss of revenue for Detroit was massive, services began to crumble and no one could move quick enough to stop the bleeding. As time passed the poorer residents made up an ever larger percentage of the population that gave the city an image of perpetual poverty.

Globalization corroded away the American manufacturing base and took most of Detroit's low education jobs which resulted in high unemployment for Detroit. Suburbs experienced low crime thanks to their high economic homogeneity and were able to put the money that would normally go to police into education which helped keep the suburbs not only afloat, but allowed them to prosper. Suburban politicians lured tech and corporate jobs from Detroit which only furthered the city's decline. The problems of Detroit are by no means unique to Detroit and can be applied to most American cities, especially those in the Midwest who have all seen decline in population. but the fact of the matter is that in the time between the 70's through the 90's the federal government didn't care for it's cities. When New York was on the verge of collapse President Ford told the city "drop dead", Reagan cut revenue sharing programs and federal aid to cities, and every president from this era subsidized suburban growth. The reason Detroit has it particularly so bad is because Detroit was the most susceptible to suburbanization. this concludes why Detroit has declined, now i'd like to write on why its coming back

First there are some things everyone aught to know, some misconceptions to clear up if you will. While Midwestern cities have declined, the metro areas of the Midwest are quite wealthy and populous. Detroit may have loss 25% of it population between 2000 and 2010 however the metro area has increased from 4.5 to 5 million and the suburban counties of Detroit are some of the wealthiest in the nation, so in a regional sense, Detroit is doing just fine. The next thing to know is that Detroit was, and always has been the flagship city of Michigan, it is the center for trade and commerce and was by no means some backwater hamlet before the auto industry came along. Detroit even today boasts the busiest international trade route in north america. the point of this paragraph was to make it clear that the city still has a lot going for it and that the biggest road blocks to revitalization is more an issue of regionalism than anything else.

thanks to high fuel costs, excessive collage debt, rising land costs in the suburbs and a new flow of federal aid to the cities many young people and empty nesters (retiring baby boomers) are beginning to move into the inner cities of america. Detroit saw its fair share of growth as its inner city doubled in population over 2000 to 2010 and continues to do so.

Detroit's regional politics have often fallen into two camps, the suburbanites who loath Detroit and blame them for ruining the once beautiful city they occupied, and the city who blame the suburbs for abandoning them and denying any responsibility. Both side have seen strong and horrible leaders and both sides have done nothing but blame the other for the last 50 years. But in 2006 we began to see a strange new phenomena emerge, a third camp comprised of those young professionals and empty nesters called regionalists, who claimed that the only way things are going to get better is if we start working together. And they have been gaining steam and wining elections like crazy. Unlike the predominantly far right suburbs and the prominently far left city the regionalists boast members across the spectrum, from the democratic mayor of Detroit, Mike Duggan to the republican Governor of the state, Rick Snyder.
